extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, empirical researchers, econometricians, USPTO analysts, and policy analysts studying patent litigation/IPR risks
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of patent- and examination-related variables to predict the likelihood a granted patent will be involved in infringement litigation or be the subject of an IPR petition, using matched case-control designs and conditional logistic regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of continuations and divisionals
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of defining this variable, we treat continuations (CONs and CIPs) and divisional applications (DIVs) identically to new applications. That is, a CON can have a first-action allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuations and divisionals are coded/treated the same as new applications in the dataset; analysts should allow for first-action allowances on continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Seniority (GS-level categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator variables related to the pay grade (at the time of allowance) of the examiner who allowed the patent: GS-12 or below, GS-13, GS-14 and above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: GS-12-and-below are non-signatory and their work is reviewed/signed by supervisors; GS-13 often have partial signatory authority and are under high scrutiny; GS-14+ are typically full-signatory/primary examiners with more independence. Expect seniority to affect allowance patterns and possibly litigation rates; include indicator for missing GS-level (~5% of sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: GS level missing indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: An indicator variable identifying patents for which information about the examiner’s pay grade was missing (roughly 5% of patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a separate indicator to avoid dropping observations with missing examiner GS-level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A count of allowed independent claims for each patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a proxy for patent scope; expected to be positively correlated with litigation. Note complication: applicants may include narrow/overlapping independent claims, so additional independent claims don't always increase scope. Examples: method, computer-readable medium, system independent claims; high-value inventions often have overlapping independent claims. Fee note: applicants are charged fees for independent claims in excess of three (currently $420 per claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words per independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The average number of words per independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis: more words per independent claim => better-defined boundaries => negatively correlated with litigation. For continuous-variable impact, assess effect by changing from 25th to 75th percentile (e.g., 79→194 words predicted to decrease odds of litigation by 20%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether any of the claims have a functional limitation, operationalized by presence of the phrases 'means for' or 'step for'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claim language lets drafters rely on specification for scope, sometimes making claims less clear; expected (in some models) to be positively associated with litigation or petitions. Note measurement caveat: functional limitations may exist without those phrases; conversely presence of phrases may not always indicate a functional limitation, but the study uses these phrases as the coding rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small entity status
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the patent was granted to a small entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically, litigated/IPR-petitioned patents are more likely to have been granted to small entities. Small-entity policies (e.g., fee discounts) may influence applicant behavior and thus downstream litigation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation history — Number of domestic parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of domestic parent applications in the patent's family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to measure extent of continuation history; litigated/IPR-petitioned patents exhibit much more extensive continuation histories (e.g., average number of domestic parents ~2.5x control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation history — Pendency from earliest parent to docketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Time (pendency) from the filing date of the earliest parent to the docketing date of the later-issued application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer family pendency is associated with higher litigation/IPR risk; e.g., litigated patents showed roughly 66–70% longer pendency from earliest parent to docketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the application claims foreign priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigated/IPR-petitioned patents are less likely to have foreign priority claims. Use both foreign priority claim indicator and 35 U.S.C. § 371 national stage entry as measures of foreign origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: 371 case (national stage entry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the application is a 35 U.S.C. § 371 national stage entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate measure of foreign-origin applications; used alongside foreign priority to capture foreign origin effects (litigated/IPR-petitioned patents less likely to be 371 entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of IDS filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) forms submitted during examination (note: count of IDS forms, not number of documents cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher IDS counts are positively and significantly related to likelihood of litigation and IPR petitions. IDS filings may indicate greater applicant involvement and perceived invention value. Use as an explanatory variable and note it's driven largely by applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of examiner interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of interviews between applicant/attorney and examiner during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More interviews correlate positively with litigation and IPR petition likelihood; may signal applicant engagement and perceived value of the patent. In some matched samples, the effect is statistically significant (e.g., ~25–40% higher counts for petitioned/litigated patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency before examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Time from docketing to allowance (examination pendency attributable to the examiner/application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer examination pendency is associated with higher litigation/IPR risk in some models (propensity-matched), but results may differ by matching approach. Interpret cautiously and control for other covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of RCEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of Request for Continued Examination (RCE) filings in the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher RCE counts are associated with increased litigation/IPR petition probability (significant in several specifications). Use as a signal of prolonged prosecution and applicant persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: At least one appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the application had at least one appeal (a decision on an appeal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of an appeal is associated with higher litigation/IPR probability (observed to be ~2% of cases but rates were ~2x higher in litigated/petitioned samples). An appeal suggests contested claim rejections and may signal value/uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAOM Allowance (First-Action On the Merits allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether the patent was allowed on the first action on the merits (first-action allowance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigated patents are less likely to have FAOM allowances; FAOM may indicate well-drafted or narrow claims, which could reduce litigation through reduced uncertainty or reduced value. Include as a prosecution-quality indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of matched case-control design
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching litigated/petitioned patents to control patents using approaches such as three-year forward-citations matching and propensity-score matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching choice affects which covariates can be included (e.g., variables used to generate propensity scores — entity size, continuation history, foreign status — are excluded from the propensity-score matched model). Analysts should compare results across matching methods for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional logistic regression for 1:1 matched samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of conditional logistic analysis (conditional maximum likelihood) when conducting matched case-control studies (especially 1-to-1 matched designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: fully stratified logistic (with matched-pair indicators) yields inconsistent MLE as number of strata increases; conditional logistic (Cox & Hinkley approach) yields consistent coefficient estimates for 1:1 matched samples. Report odds ratios from these models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odds ratio reporting and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: All results from the logistic regressions are reported as odds ratios. Odds are defined as p/(1-p). An odds ratio of 1.2 indicates a 20% increase in odds per one-unit increase; 0.8 indicates a 20% decrease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret direction and magnitude via odds ratios; present z-statistics to evaluate difference from one. For indicator variables, the odds ratio itself measures impact; for continuous variables, consider interquartile changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect-size calculation for continuous variables (25th→75th percentile)
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuous explanatory variables, impact is calculated as the model-predicted change in odds when changing the variable from its 25th percentile to its 75th percentile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: changing average words per independent claim from 79 (25th) to 194 (75th) predicted to decrease odds of litigation by 20%. Use this approach to present comparable effect sizes across continuous predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance thresholds and z-statistic guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use z-statistics to determine significance: absolute z > 1.64 indicates marginal significance, >1.96 indicates significance, and >2.58 indicates high significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report stars/notations (e.g., ***, **, *) corresponding to 1%, 5%, 10% significance levels. Provide z-statistics alongside odds ratios for full inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection and fit criteria (AIC/BIC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare models using information criteria such as Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC); lower values indicate preferred models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a model including only entity size, foreign origin, and continuation history outperformed a fuller model by BIC but slightly underperformed by AIC. Use both criteria and consider sample size/penalty differences when choosing preferred model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caveats and applicant-driven variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish variables largely under applicant control (IDS filings, interviews, first-action allowances) versus those under USPTO control; applicant behavior can drive many observed relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal interpretation should be cautious: applicant-driven indicators may reflect perceived invention value rather than examination quality. Policy implications: USPTO policies can indirectly influence applicant behavior (e.g., small-entity fee discounts, examination of progenitor apps).
